title: Sacred buildings
hookLine: cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: visit as a respectful guest

lines: A CEILING HIGHER THAN IT NEEDS TO BE.
cards: A heavy door swings shut behind you, and the street noise is gone. The ceiling is higher than it needs to be. Somewhere, someone is praying quietly, and you lower your voice without being asked.
Cathedral, mosque, temple, gurdwara, synagogue: people have built rooms like this on purpose. You don't have to share the faith of a place to honor its hush.
You only have to come in the way a guest comes into someone's home.

teach.h: JACOB: AND I KNEW IT NOT.
teach.b: First, a place that turned out to be holy. In Genesis, Jacob is on the run, sleeping in the open with a stone for a pillow.

He dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."
There's no building yet. Just a man waking up to where he is. Second, watching your step.
Ecclesiastes advises anyone entering a house of worship, in the King James words: "Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear."
Holy places often ask something of the body first: shoes off in some, heads covered in others, voices lowered. The body learns respect before the mind has words for it. Third, being a guest.
A sacred building is someone's spiritual home. A guest doesn't need to believe what the hosts believe, or pretend to.
A guest dresses with care, asks at the door what's expected, watches what others do, and doesn't photograph people at prayer without asking.
Some places welcome visitors at set hours, or have someone who will show you around.
You may not pray there, or understand everything you see. But you'll stand where other people have brought their joys and griefs, and some visitors say they can feel that weight in the room.
Jacob's words fit many first visits: a place that meant more than it looked, and I knew it not.

how: Churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras and synagogues often welcome respectful visitors; guests typically dress modestly, follow the house customs on shoes and head coverings, and ask before taking photos.

games.q: you're Jacob. you wake from a dream of a ladder reaching to heaven, in an empty place with a stone for a pillow. what do you say?
o: "surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not."
games.why: Genesis 28: Jacob wakes and says the LORD is in this place, "and I knew it not", and calls it the gate of heaven, with no building in sight.

practice: Find a picture of the inside of one sacred building, a cathedral, a mosque, a temple, a gurdwara, a synagogue, and look slowly: which way do people face, where does the eye go first, where would you stand if you walked in?
If you pray, let this be a quiet greeting to the place; if you don't, simply stand there as a guest.

wordCard.voice: Sacred buildings. Rooms made on purpose to change how you stand and speak, visited not as a tourist, but as a guest. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: as a guest. Seven days of awe: a tree, small things, water, a storm, music, a newborn, a sacred room. That's the week.
